title: Tag list helper
topic: Using `tags=()` as a default argument and rebinding with `+`
blurb: A small Python helper that appends normalized tags.
prompt: Spec: strip and lowercase `tag`, add it to `tags` if non-empty and new, and return the tuple without leaking across separate calls. Review this helper — tap a line if it breaks the spec, or let it pass.

segments.label: L3
segments.text: if not cleaned or cleaned in tags:

conclusion: AI summary: Calling `append_tag('VIP')` then `append_tag('Sale')` returns `('vip',)` and `('sale',)` — completely isolated.

diagnosis: Default container `tags=()` is created once at `def` time, so later calls leak tags from earlier calls.
Python forbids an empty tuple `()` as a default parameter value.
Using `tags=()` means callers can't pass an existing tuple like `('vip',)`.
Default `tags=()` is shared across calls, so calling `append_tag('sale')` second returns `('vip', 'sale')`.
fix: Change to `tags=None` and initialize `if tags is None: tags = ()` inside to stop leaks.
Use `tags=tuple()` in the signature so Python allocates a fresh tuple each call.
Switch the default to `tags=[]` and convert to tuple at the end.
Require callers to always pass `tags` explicitly with no default.

diagnosis: Calling `.strip().lower()` mutates `tag` in place, changing the caller's string.
Running `.strip()` before `.lower()` misses uppercase spaces at the start of `tag`.
`tag.strip().lower()` returns `None` when `tag` is already lowercase.
If `tag` has spaces in the middle like `'vip pass'`, `.strip()` removes them.
fix: Call `tag.lower().strip()` instead of `.strip().lower()`.
Clone `tag` with `str(tag)` before calling `.strip().lower()`.
Use `tag.replace(' ', '').lower()` so whitespace is handled.
Check `if tag:` before calling `.strip().lower()`.

diagnosis: `cleaned in tags` raises TypeError when `tags` is the empty tuple `()`.
Operator precedence parses `not (cleaned or cleaned in tags)`, inverting the duplicate check.
`in` checks substring membership on tuples, so `'vi'` matches `'vip'`.
Using `or` instead of `and` skips valid tags whenever `tags` is empty.
fix: Add explicit parentheses: `if (not cleaned) or (cleaned in tags):`.
Guard `if tags and cleaned in tags:` so empty `()` doesn't raise.
Replace `or` with `and` so non-empty unique tags pass through.
Convert `tags` to a `set` before checking `cleaned in tags`.

diagnosis: Returning `tags` directly returns a shared reference to the default tuple, leaking future edits.
When `cleaned` is empty, returning `tags` should return `None` instead of `()`.
Returning early leaves `cleaned` bound in the default tuple.
Returning `tags` skips converting it to a list.
fix: Return `tuple(tags)` so the default `()` isn't exposed.
Return `None` when `cleaned` is empty.
Return `()` explicitly instead of `tags`.
Return `list(tags)` for consistency.

diagnosis: Augmented assignment `tags += (cleaned,)` mutates the default `tags=()` in place, leaking `cleaned` into the next call.
Writing `(cleaned,)` with a trailing comma creates a 2-element tuple with `None` as the second entry.
Tuples are immutable in Python, so `tags += (cleaned,)` raises TypeError at runtime.
Using `+=` on a parameter modifies the caller's tuple outside the function.
fix: Replace `tags += (cleaned,)` with `tags = tags + (cleaned,)` so it stops mutating in place.
Drop the trailing comma and write `tags += (cleaned)` so it stays a 1-element tuple.
Convert to a list first with `list(tags).append(cleaned)` before returning.
Assign to a new local variable `out = (*tags, cleaned)` so `tags` isn't touched.

diagnosis: Returning `tags` returns the mutated default tuple shared with every future call.
Because tuples are immutable, line 5 was a no-op and line 6 still returns `()`.
Returning `tags` returns a nested tuple `((), 'vip')` on the first call.
Should return `cleaned` instead of `tags`.
fix: Return `tuple(tags)` to copy away from the default.
Return `(cleaned,)` directly when `tags` was empty.
Unpack `return (*tags,)` so it isn't nested.
Return `list(tags)` so callers can iterate over it.

clean_conclusion: Default `[]` leaks because lists mutate in place under `+=`. `()` is an immutable tuple, so `tags += (cleaned,)` allocates a brand-new tuple and rebinds the local name without ever touching the default.
explanation: Default `[]` leaks because lists mutate in place under `+=`. `()` is an immutable tuple, so `tags += (cleaned,)` allocates a brand-new tuple and rebinds the local name without ever touching the default.
